title: Commercial context and past dealings: editorial notes and questions
summary: Read the surrounding notes and questions alongside the principal cases. The complete assigned pages are preserved here.
notes:
Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.: This case shows how an apparently simple word can require a factual inquiry into negotiations, specialized usage, incorporated standards, and price. It connects the formation-stage question of objective assent to interpretation of an agreement both sides acknowledge.

Hurst v. W.J. Lake & Co.: Hurst gives a concrete example of contextual interpretation of numbers. Read it with Frigaliment and Nanakuli to separate proof of a usage, the parties’ connection to it, and its consistency with express language.

Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co.: Nanakuli connects interpretation, evidence of prior performance, and good-faith limits on contractual discretion. It shows why the written price clause is the beginning of an inquiry into the agreement rather than the entire inquiry.

Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.: Figgie connects interpretation and remedies: first identify the remedy the parties’ agreement contains, including trade usage, and only then decide whether that remedy remains enforceable. It demonstrates why a case needs to appear in more than one topic index.

Columbia Nitrogen Corp. v. Royster Co.: This is a major qualification to the idea that a merger clause excludes all outside evidence. The kind of evidence matters: commercial practices have a distinct place in the Code’s account of agreement.
